title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
This report demonstrates a complete linear regression workflow:
Explore Data → Specify Models → Estimate Models → Compare Models → Evaluate Assumptions → Select a Model → Interpret Results
We will use the attitude dataset to investigate associations between overall workplace rating, handling of employee complaints, opportunities to learn, and pay increases.
Our objectives are to:

Specify and estimate several plausible competing regression models.
Compare nested models using F-tests and changes in explained variance.
Evaluate overall model performance using R², adjusted R², and RMSE.
Examine regression diagnostics.
Select and interpret a preferred model.
Report results reproducibly using Quarto.

All numerical results in this document are generated directly from the analysis.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
1. Prepare the data


Code
library(carData)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)

data("attitude")

# Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
department_attitude <- attitude |>
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)

n <- nrow(department_attitude)

library(ggplot2)

# Scatterplot with a linear regression line
ggplot(data = department_attitude, aes(x = rating, y = complaints)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", col = "blue") # Adds line of best fit


Code
# Scatterplot with a linear regression line
ggplot(data = department_attitude, aes(x = rating, y = learning)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", col = "blue") # Adds line of best fit


Code
# Scatterplot with a linear regression line
ggplot(data = department_attitude, aes(x = rating, y = raises)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", col = "blue") # Adds line of best fit


The dataset contains overall workplace ratings, handling of complaints, opportunity to learn, and pay increases for 30 departments.
We use complete cases for all variables so that the candidate models are estimated using the same observations.
The final analysis includes data from 30 departments.

Research question and predictions
How are handling of complaints, opportunities to learn, and increases in pay associated with overall workplace rating?
We expect:

Departments who handle complaints better to have higher overall ratings.
Departments with more opportunities to learn to have higher overall ratings.
Departments with more substantial or frequent increases in pay to have higher overall ratings.

These are predictions about associations, not causal effects.

The regression lines shown here are bivariate relationships rather than relationships adjusted for other predictors. Thus, we can explore the distinct relationship each predictor variable (i.e., complaints, learning, and raises) has with the outcome variable (i.e., rating). The relationship between complaints and rating appear to be positive and weakly linear, approximately, as the distribution of individual department complaint scores are close to the fitted regression line. Consistent with our hypothesis, this suggests that higher a department attitudes towards the handling of employee complaints is associated with higher department ratings of the workplace. The relationship between learning and rating, however, is less linear. The relationship is still positive, where more opportunities for learning are associated with higher workplace ratings overall, though many of the individual department ratings are far from the regression line. Similarly, the relationship between raises and ratings was somewhat positively linear, where higher pay increases is associated with higher workplace ratings, but there is a lot residual distance between individual department ratings and the regression line.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
3. Specify and estimate competing models
Numerous factors contribute to the ways employees rate the workplace overall. One important factor may be the ways in which employee complaints are handled. In work environments where employee voices are not heard, concerns are not addressed, and complaints are not taken seriously or handled appropriately, it is possible that employees may feel frustrated, unseen, and as though their opinions do not matter. Further, when complaints are not handled correctly, the subject of the complaint will likely not be confronted or resolved, ultimately creating an environment that employees may not enjoy. Further, opportunities for learning may contribute to one’s rating of their workplace. The ability to expand one’s skill set, learn new things, and grow as a person may create a supportive, expansive, challenging environment which may positively contribute to an individuals attitude towards their workplace. This may account for more variation in overall workplace ratings between departments than when we exclusively consider the handling of complaints. Lastly, raises may influence one’s attitudes towards the workplace, where higher and/or more frequent increases in pay might increase employee satisfaction with their workplace. This factor may account for additional variation in overall workplace rating than when we only consider handling of complaints and opportunities for learning. As such, when exploring employee overall rating of their workplace, it is important to consider the handling of complaints, opportunities for learning, and increases in pay to understand this association.
We will fit an intercept-only model and three increasingly complex substantive models.








Model
Formula
Research rationale




M0: Null
rating ~ 1
Baseline model


M1: Complaints
rating ~ complaints
Rating varies with complaints


M2: Complaints + Learning
rating ~ complaints + learning
Learning explains additional variation


M3: Expanded
rating ~ complaints + learning + raises
Raises explains additional variation



The models are nested: each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one or more additional predictors.


Code
# Intercept-only model
mod0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = department_attitude)

# Complaints model
mod1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = department_attitude)

# Complaints + Learning model
mod2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = department_attitude)

# Expanded model
mod3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = department_attitude)

Some important interpretive distinctions:

In M0, the intercept represents the sample mean rating score.
In M1, the complaints coefficient represents the expected difference in rating associated with one increase in employees’ reported attitudes towards workplace handling of employee complaints.
In M2, the complaints coefficient represents this association after adjusting for employees’ attitudes towards opportunities for learning.
In M3, complaints and learning coefficients are additionally adjusted for employees’ attitudes towards pay increases.

In this case, we can investigate the overall workplace ratings when we account for complaints, learning, and ratings in a nested model. In M0, the intercept represents the sample mean rating score. In M1, the complaints coefficient represents the expected difference in rating associated with one increase in employees’ reported attitudes towards workplace handling of employee complaints. When we only account for complaints, we would estimate that a 1 unit increase in complaints is associated with a 0.75461 unit increase in overall workplace rating. However, when we account for complaints and learning, this relationship changes slightly. In M2, the complaints coefficient represents this association after adjusting for employees’ attitudes towards opportunities for When we account for complaints and learning, we would estimate that a 1 unit increase in complaints is associated with a 0.6435 increase in workplace rating, slightly less than the previous model. Similarly, when we account for complaints, learning, and raises, the relationship changes again as the complaints and learning coefficients are additionally adjusted for employees’ attitudes towards pay increases. In the complaints coefficient, we are now exploring the relationship between complaints and workplace rating while controlling for learning and raises. In this model, we would estimate that a 1 unit increase in complaints is associated with a 0.65349 increase in workplace rating, slightly more than the previous model, but less than M1.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
4. Compare the models
We will evaluate the models using two complementary approaches.
Nested-model F-tests determine whether the additional predictor(s) in a larger model produce a statistically significant improvement in fit.
Overall model performance describes how well each model fits the observed data.
Our main performance metrics are:

R²: Proportion of variation explained.
Adjusted R²: Explained variation adjusted for model complexity.
RMSE: Root mean squared error, expressed in rating-score units.
ΔR²: Increase in explained variation compared with the preceding model.


4.1. Conduct nested-model comparisons
Because our models are nested and estimated using the same observations, we can compare all four models in a single anova() call.


Code
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests

Model 2: rating ~ complaints
Model 3: rating ~ complaints + learning

Each row represents a model. The F-statistic and p-value on each row after the first test whether that model improves fit relative to the preceding model.
For example:

M1 versus M0 tests the contribution of complaints.
M2 versus M1 tests the additional contribution of learning.
M3 versus M2 tests the joint additional contribution of raises.

We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.


Code
tests <- tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    Residual.df = Res.Df,
    Nested.df = Df,
    Nested.F.statistic = F,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>F)`
    )




4.2. Extract overall model performance
The glance() function returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.


Code
glance0 <- glance(mod0)
glance1 <- glance(mod1)
glance2 <- glance(mod2)
glance3 <- glance(mod3)


We can then combine these results using rbind().


Code
mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Complaints",
  "M2: + Learning",
  "M3: + Raises"
)

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3
)




4.3. Combine nested tests and model performance
Because the rows in glances and tests represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using cbind().
Next, calculate the change in R² between successive models using lag().
We will also calculate RMSE directly from each model’s residuals.
Why calculate RMSE separately?
Although glance() provides a statistic called sigma, this is the residual standard error rather than the ordinary in-sample RMSE. The two use different denominators.
For consistency, we calculate RMSE explicitly as the square root of the mean squared residual.

Interpreting the combined table
Each row represents one fitted model.
The first set of statistics describes the overall performance of that model:

R²
Adjusted R²
RMSE

The second set describes its incremental improvement relative to the preceding model:

ΔR²
Nested degrees of freedom
Nested F-statistic
Nested p-value

For example, the M2 row tells us:

How much variation M2 explains overall.
How much additional variation M2 explains compared with M1.
Whether the improvement is statistically significant.

The M3 comparison tests the joint contribution of occupational category after accounting for education and income.
The M0 row has no incremental comparison because it serves as the baseline.
In this case, our model comparison table reveals an abundance of information surrounding the contribution of each predictor towards the outcome variable. First, M2 and M3 report the largest proportion of variation in rating, with an R² value of 0.708. The adjusted R² value adds more detail, as we observe an increase from M1 to M2, and a decrease from M2 to M3. This suggests that adding learning to the model account improved model fit, and adding raises to the model did not improve model fit. The ΔR² value describes how much additional variation is explained by successive models, revealing that M2 describes an additional 0.027 variation, but M3 did not explain any more variation. This may suggest that M2 is an ideal model. Notably, though M2 reports additional variation compared to M1, this addition does not produce statistically significant improvements in fit. The variation accounted for in M3 is also not statistically significant. Further, the RMSE values across M1, M2, and M3 are all relatively similar, as reductions do not appear substantially meaningfully. Therefore, between all measures of model fitness, results suggest that complaints is a primary contributor to the overall workplace rating score, while learning provides contributes slightly (and not statically significantly) and raises provides limited explanatory information.


4.5. Additional performance comparison
The performance package also provides a convenient way to compare and explore fitted models.


Code
performance_comparison <- compare_performance(
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3,
  rank = TRUE
)


We can check the performance of the most promising model, selected on the basis of comparisons of fitness statistics between nested models, by exploring the results from diagnostic plots.









These functions may include additional metrics such as AIC and BIC, which we will not focus on here. Of the diagnostic plots included, we can investigate the satisfaction of various assumptions to inform the interpretation of our findings. Several assumptions appear to be adequately satisfied. For instance, the posterior predictive check appears reasonably satisfied, as the model predicted lines generally resemble the observed data line. Regarding the model’s linearity, the reference line is approximately flat and horizontal, with only a few areas deviating from the desired shape. This suggests that the relationship between the predictors and the outcomes are adequately satisfied by the model. There are no observations that disproportionately influence the fitted model, as shown in the influential observations graphs. Lastly, the residuals appear to be approximately normally distributed, as depicted in the normality of residuals graph. The observations deviate slightly, though they do not fall too far from the line.
However, homogeneity of variance raises a potential problem. The reference line should be flat and horizontal, though the fitted line has many curves. This suggests the homoscedasticity is not sufficiently satisfied, as the residual variability is not reasonably consistent across fitted values. This problem suggests that the dispersion of errors is inconsistent, reducing confidence in the model as the reliability of various descriptive statistics is decreased.
As such, one should acknowledge the limitations of the model. While most assumptions are reasonably satisfied, one should recognize this limitation in the interpretation of the results.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
5. Select a provisional model
Model selection requires considering both statistical evidence and model complexity.
In particular, we should consider:

Whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit.
How much additional variation is explained.
Whether adjusted R² improves.
Whether RMSE meaningfully decreases.
Whether the added complexity is substantively justified.

For this demonstration, we will use adjusted R² as an initial selection criterion.
This is a convenient teaching example, not a universal rule for selecting regression models.
The provisionally selected model is M1: Complaints.
Its performance is:

R² = 0.681
Adjusted R² = 0.67
RMSE = 6.76 rating points.

We will now examine whether the selected model has important diagnostic problems.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
6. Evaluate regression diagnostics
Regression diagnostics help identify potential violations of model assumptions and unusual observations.
We will examine:

Linearity.
Residual normality.
Heteroscedasticity.
Influential observations.
Multicollinearity, where applicable.


Standard diagnostic plots





Regression diagnostic plots for the provisionally selected model




When interpreting these plots, consider:
Residuals versus fitted values
Is there evidence of curvature or systematic patterns?
Normal Q–Q plot
Do the residuals deviate substantially from a normal distribution?
Scale–location plot
Does residual variability change across fitted values?
Residuals versus leverage
Are there observations with unusually high leverage or influence?


Additional diagnostics
The performance package provides a more comprehensive diagnostic interface.
Run the following interactively in the Console:









For models with multiple predictors, you can also investigate multicollinearity:


NULL


These diagnostics should inform your final model selection.
A model with slightly better fit statistics may not be preferable if its assumptions are seriously compromised.
For the purposes of this worked example, we retain the provisionally selected model for the reporting demonstration.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
7. Report the selected model
M1 was identified as the model which provides the most defensible representation of the relationship between the workplace attitude variables and overall ratings. Though the M1 R² value was lower than the M2 and M3 values, the other measures of fitness support this model. The nested-model F-tests yielded the highest value for the M1 model, suggesting that this model greatly improved fit compared to the NULL model, while the M2 and M3 models returned much smaller F-statistic values. Between the identified predictors, complaints alone explained 68.1% of the variation in department ratings. The addition of learning and raises did not produce statistically significant improvements in model fit. In fact, the adjusted R² decreased following the addition of raises, suggesting that this predictor did not contribute sufficient explanatory value to justify increased model complexity. Moreover, M1 yielded a substantially lower RMSE value than the NULL model, and was similar to the values associated with M2 and M3. M1 also had appropriate model complexity and produced diagnostic plots which reasonably met necessary assumptions. As such, M1 was is more appropriate than the other models to describe the relationship between the workplace attitude variables and overall ratings.

7.1. Extract regression coefficients
The tidy() function extracts coefficient-level results from a fitted model.


Code
coefficient_results <- tidy(
  selected_model,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
8. Interpret the results

Overall model performance
The selected model, M1: Complaints, explains approximately 68.1% of the variation in rating within this sample.
Its adjusted R² is 0.67, and its in-sample RMSE is 6.76 rating points.
The RMSE describes the typical magnitude of the model’s fitted residuals on a root-mean-square scale.
It should not be interpreted as an estimate of out-of-sample predictive accuracy.


Interpreting constraints
Holding the other predictors constant, a one-unit increase in employee attitudes concerning handling of complaints is associated with a significant 0.75-point increase in predicted rating.


Interpreting learning
The selected model did not include learning as the addition of this predictor did not produce statistically significant improvements in model fit.


Interpreting raises
The selected model did not include raises as the addition of this predictor did not produce statistically significant improvements in model fit.


Substantive conclusions
This analysis illustrates how rating can be investigated using several competing regression models.
The model-comparison process allows us to evaluate whether additional predictors explain meaningful variation beyond simpler models.
The final model provides estimates of the associations between employee attitudes towards handling of complaints, opportunities for learning, and raises in pay and rating.
However, several limitations should be recognized:

The observations describe departments rather than individual people.
The data are observational.
Regression coefficients represent associations rather than causal effects.
Model diagnostics may reveal limitations not captured by summary fit statistics.
In-sample model performance does not establish out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
